items.text: China's Tianwan 7 reactor sent its first electricity to the grid on October 8, just over a week after it first sustained a controlled chain reaction. It is a Russian-designed VVER-1200 unit on the coast of Jiangsu province, built under a 2018 deal between Russia and China, and construction began in May 2021. Owner China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) says power will now be raised in steps, with tests at each level, before commercial operation, which was scheduled for 2026. Its twin, unit 8, is due in 2027. Once all units run, the site will have more than 9 gigawatts (GW) of capacity.

sources.title: China's Tianwan 7 connected to the grid (World Nuclear News)

items.text: Swiss voters may get the final say on new reactors. Switzerland has banned building new nuclear plants since 2018, and parliament has approved lifting that ban. A coalition led by the Greens and Social Democrats says it has handed in more than 131,800 signatures, far above the 50,000 needed, to force a national referendum on the change. If the referendum is approved, the vote could come on February 28, 2027 at the earliest. A business and utility alliance including Axpo, Alpiq and BKW has started campaigning for a yes. Switzerland's four reactors make about one third of its electricity.

sources.title: Swiss citizens may get to vote on construction of new reactors (World Nuclear News)

items.text: Westinghouse @WECNuclear hired South Korea's Hyundai Engineering & Construction to do part of the early design work, called front-end engineering design (FEED), for two large AP1000 reactors the Netherlands plans to build. The Dutch state reactor company NEO NL awarded design study contracts to EDF and Westinghouse in August; the studies take 12 to 18 months. The first phase does not depend on the site, so work can start while the government chooses one; Borssele is the cabinet's preferred location and a site choice is expected next month. The two new units are planned for around 2035.

sources.title: Westinghouse teams up with Hyundai E&C for Dutch FEED studies (World Nuclear News)

items.text: A small reactor has a first customer in Canada. BWX Technologies said on October 5 that its BANR reactor, a compact, factory-built gas-cooled design of about 22 megawatts (MW) of electricity, was picked for Prodigy Clean Energy's transportable nuclear plant at Belledune, New Brunswick. Two units would give up to 50 MW. The project is a partnership with the Pabineau and Eel River Bar First Nations, which would own it, and New Brunswick's government has signed a letter of intent to buy the power. Operation is targeted for the early 2030s; the reactor has not yet started licensing with Canada's nuclear regulator.

sources.title: BWXT's BANR Microreactor Chosen for Canadian Transportable Nuclear Power Plant Project (BWXT)
BWXT's BANR selected for Canadian project (ANS Nuclear Newswire)

items.text: Member governments of the International Energy Agency @IEA, the Paris-based body that coordinates wealthy countries' emergency oil stocks, agreed on October 7 to speed up the rest of the stock release they pledged in March and to put diesel first where they can. About 325 million barrels have gone out so far. About 100 million more were pledged but not yet released. Members still hold about 1.1 billion barrels of public emergency stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel. The same day, France said it will offer 10 million barrels of diesel from its strategic stocks to fuel distributors at cost for three months. Its prime minister said that should cut pump prices by 12 to 18 euro cents a liter. Which countries supply the 100 million barrels, and how much of it is diesel, has not been published. The IEA board meets again next week.

sources.title: Statement by IEA Executive Director on meeting of IEA Member governments on 7 October 2026 (IEA)
IEA discusses stock release, details still scant (Argus Media)
France to release 10M barrels of diesel from stocks to lower pump prices (Anadolu Agency)

items.text: Oil is back above $100. Brent, the global benchmark, rose 1% to about $101 a barrel on October 7 as traders weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and a storm in the Gulf of Mexico against more Middle East crude moving by tanker. The US Energy Information Administration @EIAgov says Brent futures started the third quarter at $72 on July 1, passed $100 on July 23 after military strikes resumed, and peaked at $109 on September 15. Some physical cargoes sold for as much as $132. Attacks on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and on tankers near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait were among the causes. EIA now expects Brent to average $105 in the last three months of 2026. The big unknown is whether shipments through the Strait of Hormuz keep recovering.

sources.title: Crude oil prices and refinery margins generally increased throughout the third quarter (EIA Today in Energy)
Short-Term Energy Outlook, October 2026, with the Winter Fuels Outlook (EIA)
Asia shares weaker, oil up as investors weigh Saudi-Houthi escalation (Reuters, via The Straits Times)

items.text: Ukraine keeps hitting Russian oil infrastructure. On October 7, Ukraine's General Staff said its October 2 drone strike on a major oil pipeline and storage facility near the village of Prosvet, in Russia's Samara region, damaged 14 large storage tanks, sections of pipeline and an automated oil station. Later that day a large fire broke out at the same site, seen in videos and in NASA satellite fire monitoring. The site includes pumping stations, tank farms and blending stations. The cause of the new fire had not been officially stated. EIA also lists Ukrainian drone attacks on Novorossiysk, one of Russia's main Black Sea oil terminals, among the supply risks that pushed prices up in September.

sources.title: Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast (The Kyiv Independent)
Crude oil prices and refinery margins generally increased throughout the third quarter (EIA Today in Energy)

items.text: Qatar may be getting ready to ship more LNG through the Strait of Hormuz. A Bloomberg analysis of satellite images and ship tracking found at least 12 empty LNG carriers owned or chartered by QatarEnergy @qatarenergy waiting near the country. Together they can carry about 1.1 million tons, roughly 2% of the world fleet's capacity. LNG traffic through Hormuz rose in September to its highest since the war began, but it is still about 75% below February. There is no guarantee the ships will sail. On Tuesday, Greece's shipping ministry was cited as saying a Greek-owned LNG carrier had been hit by an unidentified object near the waterway. QatarEnergy did not immediately comment.

sources.title: Qatar Brings Empty LNG Ships Into Gulf (Bloomberg, via Rigzone)

items.text: Global LNG supply is thin going into winter. New plants and higher output outside Qatar and the UAE have replaced about 60% of the Middle East LNG lost since March, according to Morgan Stanley analysis reported by Oil & Gas Journal. Europe's storage was about 70% full in late September, against a 10-year average of 87%. Morgan Stanley raised its fourth-quarter forecast for JKM, the Asian spot LNG price, to $27.50 per million British thermal units from $25, citing a slower Qatari restart. Shipping stays cheap because the tanker fleet is growing fast: about 55 new LNG carriers were delivered in the first seven months of 2026.

sources.title: LNG market tightens into winter as Europe pulls US cargoes, China reopens contract talks (Oil & Gas Journal)

items.text: Equinor @Equinor raised the cost estimate for Snøhvit Future, the upgrade of its Hammerfest LNG plant in Norway, to 26.5 billion Norwegian kroner (about $2.77 billion, per Reuters) on October 7. That is up from just over NOK 20 billion in December 2025 and NOK 13.2 billion when the plan was filed in 2022. The project adds onshore compression, which keeps gas flowing as the offshore field's pressure drops, and switches the plant to power from the grid. That cuts about 850,000 tonnes of CO2 a year, about 2% of Norway's emissions. Equinor blamed operating problems at the plant, weather and hard rock in a power cable tunnel. The schedule holds: compression in 2029 and grid power in 2030. The project is about 60% complete.

sources.title: Updated cost estimate for the Snøhvit Future project (Equinor)
Equinor's emissions project at LNG plant becomes increasingly costly (Reuters, via Baird Maritime)

items.text: Australia's High Court ruled 3 to 2 on October 7 that the approval of MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion in the Hunter Valley of New South Wales was invalid. It was the country's first climate change case in the High Court. The judges found the state's Independent Planning Commission failed to consider conditions to cut the emissions released when the mine's coal is sold and burned overseas. These are called scope 3 emissions, and they do not count in Australia's own climate tally. A state Greens MP said about 98% of emissions from Mount Pleasant and from the Hunter Valley Operations extension, approved a week earlier, are scope 3, and argued that approval could now be challenged. Federal environment minister Murray Watt said the ruling concerns state law and does not automatically apply to federal decisions. What happens next to the expansion is not yet settled.

sources.title: 'Lawyers should be running to courts' to stop coal approvals after landmark ruling, NSW MP says (The Guardian)

items.text: Poland's state-owned JSW, the European Union's largest producer of coking coal (the coal used to make steel), plans to shrink its workforce by 4,248 people by the end of 2026. That takes it below 16,000 from 20,135 at the end of March, a cut of about 21%. CEO Boguslaw Oleksy said most of the jobs lost would be administrative and that output would not fall. The cuts are part of a 2026 to 2035 recovery plan after years of heavy losses. A 2025 law makes it easier to close mines and offers miners large severance payments. Costs are already falling: mining a tonne cost 609 zloty (about 139 euros) in the first half of 2026, down from 778 zloty a year earlier.

sources.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs, 21% of its workforce, this year (Notes from Poland)

items.text: The auction for the Philippines' largest coal mine has hit another delay. Semirara Mining and Power Corp (SMPC), which runs the Semirara mine in Antique province, said on October 7 that the new bidding rules are unfair because they require it, and only it, to disclose its assets and hand them to the government if it bids. Its current contract ends in July 2027. SMPC also objected that bidders need no mining experience and that price is the only ranking factor. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the contract may now go to bid only in November or early December, after the last round was scrapped in September. She said the delay will not hurt supply, since the country's coal comes from Indonesia.

sources.title: SMPC: Semirara coal auction rules unfair (Philstar)

items.text: Poland's first offshore wind farm now has all its turbines. Northland Power @northlandpower said on October 7 that all 76 turbines are installed at Baltic Power, a 1.1 gigawatt (GW) project in the Baltic Sea that it owns jointly with Polish energy group ORLEN. More than a third are already generating, after first power reached the grid in July. Northland says the project is on track to start commercial operation in 2026 and costs are in line with original expectations. Once running it should make about 4 terawatt hours a year, around 3% of Poland's current electricity demand, under a 25 year contract for difference, a deal that guarantees a set price. ORLEN said about 7,000 people and 110 vessels worked on it.

sources.title: Northland's Baltic Power Offshore Wind Project Completes Installation of All 76 Turbines (Northland Power)
All Turbines Installed at Poland's First Offshore Wind Farm (offshoreWIND.biz)

items.text: China General Nuclear Power (CGN) brought its 2 GW Yangjiang Fanshi offshore wind farm in Guangdong province to full operation on September 24, and trade press reported it this week. It is China's first project to use 18 megawatt (MW) turbines at scale: 33 of its 131 turbines are that size, the largest model installed in batches in China, with rotors 292 meters across. The site reaches 81 kilometers from shore in water up to 53 meters deep. CGN expects more than 6.6 billion kilowatt hours a year, and up to 56 million from each 18 MW machine. The project also built China's first 500 kilovolt reactive power compensation station for an offshore wind farm, equipment that keeps voltage steady over the long cable run to shore.

sources.title: China's first project to use 18 MW offshore turbines at scale enters operation (China General Nuclear Power Group, in Chinese)
China's first 18-MW offshore wind power project begins operation (CGTN)
China commissions first commercial-scale offshore wind project with 18MW turbines (Windpower Monthly)

items.text: A prototype wind turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now reaches 365 meters (1,197 feet) at its blade tips, taller than the Eiffel Tower at 330 meters. Its builder, the Dresden engineering firm Gicon, calls it the world's tallest. The hub, the center of the rotor, sits at 300 meters; ordinary turbines are well below 200 meters. Gicon CEO Jochen Grossmann says winds that high are steadier and stronger, so the same machine could make more than twice as much electricity. That is the company's claim, and measuring the real gain is what the prototype is for. Internal wiring is still going in ahead of a planned inauguration on November 19. If it works, Gicon plans a wind farm of 3 to 5 extra-tall turbines.

sources.title: Wind turbine taller than the Eiffel Tower aims to boost German electricity production (AP, via Renewable Energy World)

items.text: In South Australia, Neoen started building stage one of the 346 MW Goyder North wind farm near Burra. Vestas will install 48 turbines of 7.2 MW each, and Downer will build the grid connection. It is due to start running in 2029 and make about 1.3 terawatt hours a year, roughly a 10% increase in the state's wind power. It backs a 100 MW round-the-clock supply deal with mining company BHP for its Olympic Dam, Carrapateena and Prominent Hill mines, paired with the 454 MW, 1.81 gigawatt hour Goyder Battery so supply can run around the clock. About 500 construction jobs are expected.

sources.title: Neoen breaks ground on 346MW Goyder North Wind Farm in Australia (Power Technology)
Neoen starts 346MW Goyder North construction (reNEWS)

items.text: Bangladesh approved its largest solar plant on October 7: a 442 megawatt (MW) farm with eight hours of battery storage, so solar power can be used after dark. The government's top planning committee, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, set the cost at 25 billion taka (about $200 million). The state Bangladesh Power Development Board will build it beside the 1.32 gigawatt Rampal coal plant in Bagerhat district, on about 372 hectares once set aside for a second coal unit. Work is scheduled from September 2026 to March 2029, and the storage is twice what was first planned. The country faces power shortages and aims for 20% renewable electricity by 2030.

sources.title: Bangladesh approves 442 MW solar project with eight-hour battery storage (pv magazine)

items.text: Solar panels and batteries supported 982,000 full-time jobs in the European Union in 2025, says industry group SolarPower Europe @SolarPowerEU: 874,000 in solar and 108,000 in battery storage, counted for the first time. Solar jobs rose 1%. About 85% of them are in installation; making equipment is only about 4%. Germany had the most, about 165,000, ahead of Spain and Italy. The group expects solar jobs to fall to 766,000 by 2030 even as the EU's solar fleet grows from 411 GW to 739 GW, because yearly installations are leveling off and crews are getting faster.

sources.title: Solar and storage power one million jobs in the EU (SolarPower Europe)
Solar and storage accounted for nearly 1 million EU jobs in 2025 (pv magazine)

items.text: Researchers at Australia's University of New South Wales (UNSW) and Chinese module maker UtmoLight reached a certified 23.5% efficiency on a 30 by 30 centimeter perovskite solar module, beating the previous benchmark by 0.6 percentage points. Perovskites are a family of crystal materials being developed for solar cells, and materials that work on a tiny lab cell often behave differently at larger sizes. The team dropped a nickel oxide layer that can react with the perovskite, which removes a manufacturing step. Next they want a full-size module of 2.8 square meters in the coming months, aiming for about 18% to 19%.

sources.title: UNSW leverages industry partnership to set large-scale perovskite PV efficiency world record (UNSW)
UNSW and UtmoLight set 23.5% efficiency record for large-area perovskite solar submodule (PV Tech)

items.text: Australia's home batteries are pulling rooftop solar along with them. Analyst SunWiz counted 311.8 MW of small solar systems (up to 100 kilowatts) registered in September, up 7% on August and well above about 240 MW a year earlier. The federal Cheaper Home Batteries rebate requires a battery to be paired with solar, and more small solar has now gone in so far in 2026 than in all of 2025. Home battery installs reached about 966.5 megawatt hours in September, and the average new battery is now 26.3 kilowatt hours. Queensland led with 91.8 MW of new solar.

sources.title: Australia's rooftop installs rise on back of battery rebate scheme (pv magazine)

items.text: Google @Google signed a 20-year deal with Constellation @ConstellationEG to pay for uprates at 11 reactors across six plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. An uprate means squeezing more power out of a machine that already runs. The target is about 890 megawatts of new output on the PJM grid, the regional market that covers 13 states. Constellation says that is more than $4.3 billion of its own investment. The first extra watts are expected by 2028. The full 890 megawatts are aimed at before the end of 2032. They also signed a separate 15-year deal covering 2,700 megawatts of Constellation's existing fleet. No power price was published. Announced October 6.

sources.title: Google and Constellation Announce Landmark Agreement to Bring 890 MW of New Nuclear Capacity to PJM Grid (Constellation release)
Why we're backing America's existing nuclear plants (Google)

items.text: The Department of Energy @ENERGY offered Vistra a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion for uprates and modernization at Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania and Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio. Vistra is a power company based in Irving, Texas. It owns plants and sells electricity. Its nuclear fleet is Comanche Peak in Texas, plus those three plants in Pennsylvania and Ohio, which came with the Energy Harbor deal in 2024. It is not a reactor designer. It runs the machines and sells the watts. The package would add about 433 megawatts and keep nearly 4 gigawatts of existing nuclear on the grid, with an option later for Comanche Peak. Conditional means the money is not wired. Vistra still has to clear technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions. Announced October 5.

sources.title: Energy Department Announces $4.2 Billion Investment to Boost Nuclear Power in Pennsylvania and Ohio (DOE)
Vistra Completes Energy Harbor Acquisition (Vistra)
DOE offers Vistra loan for reactor upgrades and uprates (World Nuclear News)

items.text: Fuel loading at Palisades in Michigan stopped after one used assembly tilted in the core. Holtec @holtecintl says the grapple had already let go when the assembly shifted and stuck at a tilt. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission @NRCgov says the rods are intact. An NRC spokesperson has said there was no release and no one was hurt. Holtec asked the NRC on September 30 for a license amendment so crews can move that assembly to the spent fuel pool with custom gear. The NRC opened a public comment opportunity on October 6. Holtec has not given a new restart date. Reports say its power contract calls for supply by March 2027. That date now depends on getting this assembly out.

sources.title: NRC Reviewing Palisades License Amendment Request, Public Comment Opportunity Open (NRC, Palisades plant page)
News Releases 2026: S-26-007, NRC Reviewing Palisades License Amendment Request (NRC)
Palisades restart delayed (Nuclear Engineering International)
Incident pauses Palisades fuel loading; plant connected to switchyard (ANS Nuclear Newswire)

items.text: The United States and South Korea outlined Project Power, a framework for eight large reactors in the United States: six Westinghouse @WECNuclear AP1000s and two Korean APR1400s. The Commerce Department fact sheet, issued September 30, puts the package at $120 billion, $100 billion for construction and $20 billion held as contingency. Sites are not picked. Schedules and contracts are not signed. Seoul said this week the project is likely to take a real shape around 2028. It is a blueprint, not a pour.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: Korea and the United States Announce Historic Strategic Investment Projects (U.S. Department of Commerce)
U.S. Nuclear Project to Take Shape Around 2028, Seoul Says (Seoul Economic Daily)
USA, South Korea targeting six AP1000 and two APR1400 units (World Nuclear News)

items.text: Tropical Storm Isaias forced offshore producers in the Gulf to stop pumping. As of midday Wednesday, October 7, about 511,619 barrels a day of oil, about 25% of Gulf offshore output, was offline, based on operator reports to the Marine Minerals Administration, the federal office that tracks offshore drilling. A day earlier the figure was 9.24%. Shutting in means closing safety valves below the sea floor until the storm passes. It is a standard precaution, not damage. Chevron @Chevron and Shell were evacuating staff from several platforms. The Gulf supplies around 15% of US crude. Forecasters expected Isaias to become a hurricane on Thursday and approach the coast on Friday, toward a stretch from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle that includes several large refineries. How long the oil stays offline depends on the storm's path.

sources.title: US Gulf operators shut-in output before storm: Update (Argus Media)
MMA Monitors Gulf of America Oil and Gas Activities in Response to Invest 92L (Marine Minerals Administration, BSEE newsroom)

items.text: The Energy Information Administration @EIAgov, the government's energy statistics office, raised its oil price outlook on October 6. It now expects Brent, the global benchmark crude, to average $105 a barrel in the last three months of 2026. That is $14 higher than its forecast a month ago. It sees Brent falling to $84 next year. US pump prices jumped in September: gasoline averaged $4.35 a gallon and diesel $6.29. Diesel is the tightest spot. East Coast stocks of diesel and heating oil fell 32% below their usual level for September. Homes that heat with oil, about 3% of households and mostly in the Northeast, face prices more than 30% above last winter. The forecast assumes Middle East oil flows stay limited through the end of the year.

sources.title: Short-Term Energy Outlook, October 2026, with the Winter Fuels Outlook (EIA)

items.text: Chevron @Chevron agreed on October 6 to hand its stake and general partner role in Hess Midstream back to that company, along with its oil gathering pipelines in Colorado's DJ Basin. Hess Midstream runs the pipelines and processing plants that serve Chevron's wells in North Dakota's Bakken field; Chevron inherited the stake when it bought Hess in 2025. In return Chevron gets $200 million in cash and cheaper, longer contracts: fees go down, the deals run through 2045, and Chevron expects its Bakken pipeline costs per barrel to fall about 50%. Chevron will book a one-time after-tax loss of about $3 billion to $4 billion at closing and take about $3.7 billion of Hess Midstream debt off its books. Hess Midstream expects Bakken volumes to dip about 5% in 2027 as Chevron drills less. The deal still needs regulatory approvals and is expected to close by the end of 2026.

sources.title: Chevron to Divest its Ownership Interests in Hess Midstream and DJ Basin Crude Midstream Assets (Chevron release, SEC Form 8-K Exhibit 99.1)
Chevron restructures Bakken midstream agreements, transfers Hess Midstream stake (Oil & Gas Journal)

items.text: The Supreme Court heard arguments on October 5 in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. Boulder County, Colorado, is suing Suncor and ExxonMobil in state court to make them pay part of the local costs of climate change. The companies argue federal law keeps state courts from hearing cases like this. If the companies win, the ruling could also end dozens of similar suits by states and cities. If Boulder wins, its case goes back to state court. Justice Samuel Alito stepped aside, so eight justices will decide. After the roughly two-hour hearing, it was not clear which way the court was leaning. No ruling has been issued.

sources.title: US supreme court hears big oil's bid to block climate damage lawsuits (The Guardian)

items.text: Tropical Storm Isaias also cut Gulf gas. About 350 million cubic feet a day of offshore gas, roughly 16% of Gulf output, was offline as of midday October 7, based on operator reports to the Marine Minerals Administration. The offshore Gulf is only about 5% of US gas supply, so the national hit is small. The bigger worry is the LNG export plants on the coast, where gas is chilled into a liquid for shipping overseas. Natural Gas Intelligence reported that the forecast track could miss most Gulf Coast LNG capacity, while the Coast Guard ordered storm preparations at ports on the lower Mississippi River.

sources.title: US Gulf operators shut-in output before storm: Update (Argus Media)
MMA Monitors Gulf of America Oil and Gas Activities in Response to Invest 92L (Marine Minerals Administration, BSEE newsroom)
Isaias Track Skirts Most Gulf LNG as Coast Guard Sets Storm Conditions (Natural Gas Intelligence)

items.text: The Energy Information Administration @EIAgov expects homes that heat with natural gas or propane, about half of US households, to spend less on average this winter than last. Homes on electric heat should pay slightly more. EIA forecasts the Henry Hub price, the main US gas benchmark, to average $3.16 per million British thermal units in 2027, 9% below 2026. The reason: production growth keeps storage above average even as LNG exports rise. The forecast assumes national winter temperatures close to last winter and the 10-winter average. A colder winter would change the math.

sources.title: Short-Term Energy Outlook, October 2026, with the Winter Fuels Outlook (EIA)

items.text: Europe is pulling harder on American LNG. About 57% of US LNG exports went to Europe in September, up from 53% in August, according to Morgan Stanley analysis reported by Oil & Gas Journal. US feedgas, the gas flowing into export plants, rose about 6% from August as Freeport LNG recovered from an outage. Europe needs the cargoes: EU gas storage was about 70% full in late September, compared with 82% a year earlier and a 10-year average of 87%. China, which had stepped back from US deals, is showing signs of returning to long-term US contracts.

sources.title: LNG market tightens into winter as Europe pulls US cargoes, China reopens contract talks (Oil & Gas Journal)

items.text: ConocoPhillips @conocophillips signed a 20-year deal to buy 1.0 million tonnes a year of LNG from Venture Global, starting in 2030. Venture Global's first three LNG projects, Calcasieu Pass, Plaquemines LNG and CP2 LNG, are in Louisiana on the Gulf coast. It says it has more than 100 million tonnes a year of capacity in production, construction or development. Announced October 6.

sources.title: Venture Global and ConocoPhillips play the long game with 20-year LNG pact (Offshore Energy)

items.text: Clearway Energy Group closed financing and started building the Swan Energy Center, a 650 megawatt (MW) solar farm on former strip-mined land in Bates County, Missouri, its first project in the state. The $1.5 billion project is financed by banks led by CIBC, DNB and National Australia Bank, and sells its power under a 20 year contract. It should start running in 2028 and make enough electricity for about 200,000 homes. Clearway says it will use American-made panels. Blattner Energy is building it, with up to 500 jobs at peak, and a 30 year payment deal with the county is set to bring in more than $80 million for schools and services.

sources.title: Clearway Closes Financing and Begins Construction on 650 MW Swan Energy Center in Missouri (Clearway Energy Group)
Clearway Starts Construction of 650-MW Solar Facility in Missouri (POWER Magazine)

items.text: Another former mine site is turning solar. Zelestra closed a $350 million loan for its 203 MW Reclamation Solar project on former coal mining land in Gibson County, Indiana. Its power is sold to Meta, the Facebook parent, which BloombergNEF says was the world's largest buyer of new clean power contracts in 2025. The project is under construction and due to start running at the end of 2027. Lenders are CIBC, BBVA and Societe Generale. Indiana has about 7.2 gigawatts of solar today and is expected to add 13.4 more over five years.

sources.title: Zelestra closes US$350 million financing at 203MW PV plant in Indiana backed by Meta (PV Tech)

items.text: Japanese solar maker Toyo celebrated on October 6 the expansion of its module assembly plant in Humble, Texas, which can now make 2 gigawatts (GW) of panels a year. It plans a $357 million addition: a 1.5 GW line making heterojunction cells, the parts inside each panel that turn light into electricity, expected by early 2028 with about 400 workers on site. A Commerce Department official at the event praised its pledge to use only US polysilicon, the raw material for cells. An open question: Commerce is investigating whether cells from Ethiopia, where Toyo runs its largest cell factory (4 GW), dodge tariffs on Chinese solar goods. Toyo says its wafers come from Indonesia using mostly US polysilicon and is asking for guidance.

sources.title: Toyo cuts the ribbon on its newly-expanded solar factory in Texas (pv magazine)

items.text: Farm solar grants just got much harder to win. New US Department of Agriculture rules for the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) bar grants for systems that make more power than the farm uses, for projects on cropland, and for parts from countries the government calls foreign adversaries. Farmers must now run a system for a year before they can apply, and grants are capped at a quarter of the cost, down from half. The rules also hit awards already granted but not yet paid. More than two-thirds of REAP grants have gone to solar. Farmers and advocates, represented by Earthjustice and the Environmental Law and Policy Center, sued days before the rules came out.

sources.title: The USDA just made it way harder for farmers to get grants for solar (Canary Media)

items.text: Offshore wind developer US Wind @USWindInc has given up its plan to make turbine parts at Sparrows Point near Baltimore, at least for now. It handed its lease at the Tradepoint Atlantic site to Anduril Industries, which plans a $3.7 billion shipyard there. The steel plant was meant to make towers and monopiles, the giant steel tubes driven into the seabed, and to create hundreds of jobs; the Trump administration had already pulled $47.4 million in federal grants for it. CEO Jeff Grybowski said on October 6 that US Wind's plans are delayed by legal disputes and federal uncertainty. Its only project, off Ocean City, Maryland, is still in court over its federal permit, which the government has said it wants to revoke.

sources.title: US Wind pulls out of wind turbine manufacturing at Sparrows Point (Maryland Matters)
